beats.text: Boston's Black history is still standing. You just have to know where to look.
In 1770, outside this building, British soldiers killed five men in the Boston Massacre.
One was Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Indigenous descent.
On Beacon Hill, Black Bostonians built this meeting house in 1806.
It's considered the oldest Black church building still standing in America.
Frederick Douglass spoke here. In 1863, men signed up here for the 54th Massachusetts.
Next door, in 1835, Boston opened a school for Black children only.
Black families fought back, with petitions, a boycott, and a lawsuit.
In 1855, Massachusetts banned segregated public schools.
Nearby, Lewis and Harriet Hayden, who had escaped slavery, sheltered freedom seekers in this house.
And facing the State House, this memorial honors the 54th, one of the first Black regiments of the Civil War.
The city changed around them. The history is still here.
Follow The Black History Room for one story a day.

facts.claim: On 5 March 1770 British soldiers killed five men outside the Old State House (King Street).
Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Indigenous ancestry, was one of them.
facts.note: Often called 'the first' killed; that ranking is traditional, so the script doesn't use it.

facts.claim: African Meeting House built 1806, by Black Bostonians (funds raised by Cato Gardner and others; mostly Black craftsmen).
Considered the oldest Black church building still standing in the US.
facts.note: NPS wording: 'considered the oldest extant Black church building in America'. Script keeps 'considered'.

facts.claim: Frederick Douglass spoke there; 1863 recruitment post for the 54th Massachusetts.
Abiel Smith School opened 1835 for Black children (segregated).
Petitions, a boycott and a lawsuit (Roberts) against segregated schools.
Massachusetts banned segregated public schools in 1855.
Lewis and Harriet Hayden escaped slavery and sheltered freedom seekers at 66 Phillips Street.
Shaw / 54th Memorial on Boston Common facing the State House, unveiled 31 May 1897; the 54th was one of the first Black regiments of the Civil War.
